analysis.one_liner: Lets people take sexual assault or harassment claims to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it with bipartisan sponsorship in November 2021, but the full Senate never voted; an identical House bill became law in March 2022.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of workers and consumers sign contracts — job offers, app terms of service — that require any dispute to be settled in private arbitration rather than court, and that waive the right to join a class action. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable, at the victim's choice, when the dispute involves sexual assault or sexual harassment. The person alleging the conduct could then file a lawsuit in court or join a class action if they want to. The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee unanimously-style with bipartisan sponsorship and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never took it up before the 117th Congress ended — the same policy became law instead through an identical House bill signed in March 2022.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, patients, and students who signed arbitration agreements before any dispute arose. They gain the choice to take sexual assault or sexual harassment claims to a public courtroom and to join class or collective actions, instead of being funneled into a private arbitration process where proceedings are confidential, damages can be lower, and each person must argue alone.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers with harassment or assault claims

how_it_helps.text: At the election of the person alleging sexual assault or sexual harassment, a predispute arbitration agreement cannot be enforced against that claim, so the case can be filed in federal, state, or tribal court.
The bill also invalidates predispute class-action waivers for these claims, so groups of workers or consumers can sue together rather than one at a time.

A court, not an arbitrator, decides whether the law applies to a given agreement, closing a common path companies used to have an arbitrator — rather than a judge — rule on the enforceability of the arbitration clause.
The protection applies to any dispute or claim that arises on or after the date of enactment, so it covers future hires and future contract signers immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Companies across the economy that put mandatory arbitration and class-action waiver clauses in employment and consumer contracts. They lose the ability to keep sexual assault and harassment claims out of court and out of class actions, and they face public lawsuits and larger combined liabilities.

drawbacks.text: The committee-reported version removed the introduced version's exception for collective bargaining agreements, so a union contract's arbitration provision can be overridden when an individual employee elects to go to court over a sexual assault or harassment claim — a change some union allies saw as intruding on negotiated agreements.

Court cases are slower, more expensive to litigate, and more public than arbitration. The bill does not ban arbitration — the alleging party chooses the forum — but victims who valued the privacy, speed, or lower cost of arbitration lose access to it as the default.

The bill leaves every other type of forced arbitration clause untouched: wage disputes, discrimination on other grounds, and consumer claims not involving sexual assault or harassment remain subject to predispute arbitration agreements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is clear and modest: victims gain a real choice of forum and the option of class action, and companies lose a tool for resolving sexual misconduct claims privately and one at a time. The main honest objections are the removal of the union-contract exception in the committee version and the higher cost and exposure of court for some claimants. On balance the bill is well-targeted — it only applies when the victim elects court, and only to these specific types of claims.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it with a bipartisan substitute amendment and put it on the Senate calendar in November 2021, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended; the identical House companion bill cleared both chambers and was signed into law in March 2022 instead.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 14, 2021, by Senator Gillibrand with 17 original cosponsors from both parties, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
On November 4, 2021, the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On November 17, 2021, Senator Durbin reported the bill out of committee with the substitute amendment, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 169).
No further action was taken: the bill never received a Senate floor vote and died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and the public came out ahead in the end, because the identical House companion bill passed both chambers and was signed into law in March 2022, making forced arbitration of sexual assault and harassment claims unenforceable nationwide. Companies that use mandatory arbitration clauses gained nothing lasting from the Senate bill's death — only a few months of delay — though they succeeded for those months in keeping the policy off the Senate floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers — the policy became law anyway

for.name: Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 14, 2021, and recruited cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original sponsor and reported it out of the Judiciary Committee favorably with a substitute amendment on November 17, 2021.

for.name: Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Joined Gillibrand as a lead original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never called S. 2342 up for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the Legislative Calendar in November 2021; the Senate instead took up the identical House companion bill, which passed and became law in March 2022.

sides.party_line_note: This was not a partisan fight: the bill was introduced with 7 Republicans among 18 original sponsors, drew 10 of 50 Senate Republicans and 18 of 48 Senate Democrats as cosponsors, cleared the Judiciary Committee without recorded opposition, and no senator ever voted against it — no roll call was ever held.

industries.industry: Employers that require workers to sign mandatory arbitration agreements
industries.note: These companies lose the ability to force sexual assault and harassment claims into private arbitration and to block workers from joining class actions. Public court cases also expose conduct that confidential arbitration would have kept hidden, which is why the industry interest runs against the people the bill protects.

industries.industry: Gig platforms, hotels, health care and long-term care providers, and other consumer-facing firms
industries.note: The bill's definitions cover not just workplace claims but also misconduct conditioning consumer, health care, or long-term care benefits on sexual activity, so consumer-facing companies lose forced arbitration for these claims too.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and the alternative dispute resolution industry
industries.note: Sexual assault and harassment claims can no longer be routed to paid private arbitrators under predispute agreements, shrinking a significant stream of arbitration business.
